title: Zhaozhou's mu
hook: a monk asks if a dog has Buddha-nature. the teacher answers with one syllable.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the koan, a question that won't let you be clever. Your line was one hand. Did a sound bring the question back? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-four.

A monk bows to the old Chinese teacher Zhaozhou and asks a question that seems to have a ready answer. The monk has heard the teaching that living beings have Buddha-nature, the capacity to wake up. So he points at the humblest example he can find. Does a dog have Buddha-nature, or not? The expected answer is yes. Zhaozhou says one syllable: mu. In Chinese and Japanese, it means something like no, or not, or there isn't. That's the whole exchange. A question, a single word, and a puzzle that has kept students sitting ever since. Today is that one word.
screen: `DOES A DOG HAVE BUDDHA-NATURE?` → `THE EXPECTED ANSWER: YES.` → `ZHAOZHOU: MU.`

segments.voice: Yesterday we met the koan in general. Today, one in particular. In the collection called The Gateless Gate, gathered by the Chinese teacher Wumen, Zhaozhou's mu is the first case. Here's how to turn it over. First, the surface. Read flatly, Zhaozhou seems to contradict the teaching the monk was repeating. If everything has Buddha-nature, why say no? That's exactly the hook. The no doesn't fit, so the mind can't file it away. Second, it isn't a vote on dogs. Zen teachers say the point isn't a yes or no about animals. Some records even have Zhaozhou answering the same question differently on another day, with a yes. That alone suggests the word is doing something other than giving information. Third, Wumen's comment. Right after the case, he tells the student how to work on it, and his pictures are vivid. In paraphrase: put your whole body into this mu, day and night. Don't take it as nothing, and don't take it as the opposite of something. It's like swallowing a red-hot iron ball you can't spit out. Fourth, what's left. Wumen's promise, again paraphrased, is that when the work ripens, inside and outside become one, and the student knows it the way someone who can't speak knows their own dream. So mu ends up less like an answer and more like a door. That's why the book is called The Gateless Gate. One syllable, breathed, until it stops being a word about something and is just there.
screen: `THE FIRST CASE IN THE GATELESS GATE.` · `THE NO DOESN'T FIT.` · `NOT A VOTE ON DOGS.` · `A RED-HOT IRON BALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: breathe mu. Sit upright, eyes soft. Let the breath come in on its own. On each out-breath, silently, let the syllable ride all the way out: muuu. Don't think about what it means. Don't make it yes or no. When your mind wanders, the next out-breath is another mu. Another day, you might try three minutes. Today, the two the bell gives. The bell holds the time.
Zhaozhou's mu. A teacher's one-syllable answer, something like no, to a monk's question about a dog. The first case in The Gateless Gate. Today's word.
Your line: mu. Today, when your mind rushes to a quick yes or no, pause, and let one quiet out-breath of mu go first. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: In Rinzai and some other Zen lineages, students are often given mu as a first koan and work on it during sitting, breathing the syllable and bringing their response to a teacher.

fork.setup: you're the monk. you've heard all beings have Buddha-nature, and you ask whether a dog has it. what does Zhaozhou say?
fork.reveal: one syllable, mu: something like no. it doesn't fit the teaching, and that's what makes it a koan.

original.note: Chinese and Japanese: no, not, there isn't. Zhaozhou's one-syllable answer.

trapdoor: what you thought: Zhaozhou said dogs don't have Buddha-nature.
what it means: a no that doesn't fit the teaching, given so it can't be filed away, worked on as a koan.
what a scholar hears: case one of The Gateless Gate, with Wumen's comment: put your whole body into mu, like a red-hot iron ball.

sources.ref: The Gateless Gate (Wumenguan / Mumonkan), case 1, with Wumen's comment
the record of Zhaozhou (other versions of the dog question)

notes: Case 1 and Wumen's comment are paraphrased (whole body into mu, day and night; not nothingness, not being/non-being; red-hot iron ball; inside and outside become one; like a mute person who has had a dream). Confirm wording and that no protected translation is echoed too closely.
The claim that other records show Zhaozhou answering 'yes' to the same question (e.g., the Book of Equanimity, case 18) is stated as 'some records'; confirm.
'Mu' glossed as 'no, not, there isn't': a meaning, not an etymology. Confirm.
The outline practice is three minutes; the app sit is two, so three minutes is offered as an optional next step.
